title: The missing DNA strand
question: A DNA strand reads 5′–A T G C–3′. What is its complementary strand written in the opposite direction, 3′ to 5′?
explanation: A pairs with T, and G pairs with C. The complementary strand runs antiparallel, so 5′–A T G C–3′ pairs with 3′–T A C G–5′.

title: From DNA to RNA
question: An RNA polymerase reads the DNA template 3′–T A C G A A–5′. Which RNA strand does it build 5′ to 3′?
options: A U G C U U
T A C G A A
A T G C T T
explanation: The RNA is 5′–A U G C U U–3′. It is complementary and antiparallel to the DNA template; RNA uses U where DNA uses T.

title: Reading three letters at a time
question: Using the standard genetic code, an mRNA reads 5′–AUG GCU UAA–3′ starting at AUG. What does it specify before translation stops?
explanation: AUG encodes methionine, GCU encodes alanine and UAA is a stop codon in the standard genetic code. Stop ends translation rather than adding an amino acid.

title: One codon changes
question: In the standard genetic code, a codon changes from GAA to GAG. What happens to its amino acid?
explanation: Both GAA and GAG encode glutamate in the standard genetic code. This single-base change is synonymous for the amino-acid sequence, though it may have other effects.

title: One letter in a codon
question: In the standard genetic code, a codon changes from GAA to GUA. What happens to the encoded amino acid?
explanation: GAA encodes glutamate and GUA encodes valine in the standard genetic code. This substitution changes one amino acid in this example.

title: A codon changes
question: In the standard genetic code, a codon changes from UAU to UAA. What happens at that position?
explanation: UAU encodes tyrosine, while UAA is a stop codon in the standard genetic code. If translated in this reading frame, the new stop ends translation at that point.

title: One extra letter shifts the groups
question: A message is read AUG | GAA | CCA. Insert A immediately after AUG. How are the next complete triplets grouped?
explanation: Inserting one base gives AUGAGAACCA. Reading from the same start produces AUG | AGA | ACC, with one trailing base; the reading frame after the insertion has shifted.

title: A message gets edited
question: A simplified RNA has exon ACG, an intron UUU, then exon GGA. If the intron is removed, what remains in this example?
explanation: In this schematic example the intron UUU is removed and exons ACG and GGA are joined. Real splice sites are specified by surrounding sequence signals and machinery.

title: One transcript, two messages
question: A pre-mRNA has exons A, B and C. One splice pattern joins A–B–C; another skips B. What is the second message?
explanation: Alternative splicing can include or omit particular exons. Here, skipping exon B joins A to C, so one pre-mRNA can produce different mature RNA sequences.

title: What survives the copy?
question: During semiconservative DNA replication, what does each newly formed double helix contain?
options: One original strand and one new strand
explanation: The two original strands separate and each acts as a template. Each resulting double helix contains one original strand and one newly synthesised complementary strand.

title: Copied but not yet separated
question: A cell has two unreplicated chromosomes. After DNA replication, before sister chromatids separate, how many chromosomes and chromatids are there?
explanation: Each chromosome is copied into two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. Before separation, this model has two chromosomes and four chromatids; each X stands for a duplicated chromosome.

title: One cell divides into two
question: A model cell has two chromosomes. After ordinary mitosis and cytokinesis, how many chromosomes are in each daughter cell?
explanation: After DNA replication, mitosis separates sister chromatids. With normal separation, each daughter in this model receives one copy of each chromosome: two per cell.

title: Four cells from one
question: A diploid model cell has one pair of homologous chromosomes (2n = 2). After meiosis, how many chromosomes are in each of its four cells?
explanation: Meiosis separates homologues and then sister chromatids. With normal separation, each of the four haploid cells in this 2n = 2 model receives one chromosome. Crossing over is omitted here.
